title: Container Escape
summary: Container escape is the class of techniques by which a process confined to a container reaches the underlying host, another tenant's container, or the cluster control plane, converting a workload compromise into infrastructure compromise. Containers share the host kernel, so the boundary is enforced by kernel features such as namespaces, control groups, capabilities, mandatory access control profiles and seccomp filters rather than by a hypervisor, and escape generally follows from a configuration or kernel flaw that weakens those controls. Recurring categories include privileged containers that hold effectively all capabilities and device access, containers mounting the host filesystem or the container runtime socket, excessive Linux capabilities combined with writable host paths, host namespace sharing for networking or process identifiers, kernel vulnerabilities reachable from within a container, and misconfigured runtime or orchestration components that trust client input excessively. The consequences of a successful escape are severe because the host usually holds credentials: node identity, cluster service account tokens, cloud instance role credentials reachable through the metadata endpoint, and secrets mounted for other workloads. Defensive practice therefore concentrates on preventing the conditions rather than only detecting the technique: forbid privileged mode and host path mounts, drop capabilities, run read-only root filesystems, apply seccomp and mandatory access control, isolate with user namespaces or sandboxed runtimes, restrict access to the runtime socket, and assume that any workload with host access has already compromised the node.
objectives: You will be able to explain why containers share the host kernel and how namespaces, capabilities and mandatory access control form the boundary.
You will be able to identify workload configurations that make escape trivial, including privileged mode, host paths and runtime socket mounts.
You will be able to design admission policy that blocks the preconditions for escape before deployment.
You will be able to describe what credentials and mounted secrets become reachable after a node is compromised.
You will be able to triage container escape indicators such as host namespace access and unexpected device usage.
You will be able to rank escape paths by realistic exploitability and business impact for a report.

beginner.definition: A container escape happens when a program trapped inside a container breaks out and reaches the machine underneath it. Containers share the same operating system kernel (the core of the system), so the wall between them is thinner than a full virtual machine. A mistake in settings or in the kernel can let someone step outside.
beginner.whyItMatters: If a container escape succeeds, the attacker is no longer stuck in one small app. They can reach the host machine, other customers' containers, or the cluster control plane. The host often holds valuable keys, such as cloud credentials and tokens for other services. One escape can turn a small problem into a whole-platform problem.
howItWorks: An attacker first gets code running inside a container, often through a bug in the app.
They look for weak settings, such as running in privileged mode, which grants almost full control.
They also check for the host disk or the runtime socket being mounted inside the container.
Using that access, they try to read host files, kernel features, or the cloud metadata endpoint.
If it works, they can steal node credentials and move to other workloads in the cluster.
Defenders prevent this by blocking privileged containers and host mounts before deployment.
beginner.example: Picture a hotel. Each guest room is a container, and the corridor and master keys belong to the host. Normally a guest stays in their room. But if the room door was fitted badly, the guest can step into the corridor, try other doors, and perhaps reach the staff office with the master key cabinet. That is a container escape.
takeaways: Containers share the host kernel, so the boundary depends on correct settings.
Privileged mode and host mounts are the most common escape preconditions.
Block risky settings at deployment time, not only after an alert.
